title: Sherlock and Array
directAnswer: Find an index i where the sum of everything to its left equals the sum of everything to its right; print 'YES' if one exists, else 'NO'. Compute the total once, then sweep left to right keeping a running leftSum. At each i the rightSum is total − leftSum − arr[i]; if leftSum == rightSum you've found a pivot. That's a single O(n) pass with O(1) extra space.

remember.pattern: Total minus running prefix gives the suffix in O(1)
remember.formula:
total = sum(arr)
left = 0
for i in 0..n-1:
    right = total - left - arr[i]
    if left == right: return "YES"
    left += arr[i]
return "NO"
rules: The pivot element itself belongs to **neither** side — that's why rightSum subtracts both `left` and `arr[i]`.
A single-element array is always **YES**: left and right are both empty sums = 0.
Update `left` **after** the comparison, so at index i it holds the sum of strictly-left elements.
Compute `total` **once**; recomputing the right sum each step is the O(n²) trap.
Equality can hold even with the pivot being large — only the two *sides* must match, the pivot is free.
whenToUse: Find a split/pivot point where two running aggregates balance
Equilibrium-index style questions on a 1-D array
Any 'left part equals right part' check you can do in one sweep
antiSignals: You need the actual partition values, not just existence → still one pass but return i
Negative numbers with a 'first/last' tie-break requirement → be careful which index you return
Repeated queries after updates → a Fenwick/segment tree beats re-sweeping
remember.takeaway: Keep a running prefix sum and derive the suffix as total − prefix − current. That O(1) suffix lookup turns a quadratic 'compare both sides at every index' into a single linear sweep — the core equilibrium-index trick.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you avoid recomputing the right-hand sum from scratch at every index by maintaining a running left sum and deriving the right sum as total − left − current in O(1).
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Including the pivot element in one of the sides, recomputing the suffix sum each iteration (O(n²)), or mishandling the single-element case.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the invariant explicitly: 'after processing index i, left holds the sum strictly before i+1.' Note the single-element YES case and that the pivot is excluded from both sides before writing code.

problemStatement:
Watson gives Sherlock an array of integers. He asks whether there exists an index such that the sum of the elements to the **left** of that index equals the sum of the elements to the **right** of that index.

For each query, print `YES` if such an index exists, otherwise print `NO`. The element at the chosen index is counted on neither side.
constraints: There may be more than one valid index; you only need to know if at least one exists
understanding: We want a pivot index i that splits the array into a left part (indices 0..i−1) and a right part (indices i+1..n−1) with equal sums; arr[i] itself is in neither part. Because the total is fixed, knowing the running left sum gives the right sum instantly: right = total − left − arr[i]. Sweep once and check equality at each index.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the pivot element included in either side?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — it sits between the two sides and counts toward neither. The right sum is total minus left sum minus the pivot value.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about a single-element array?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: It's a YES. The only index has empty left and right, both summing to 0, which are equal.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can values be negative or zero?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Per these constraints values are positive, but the running-sum logic works unchanged for negatives — don't write code that assumes positivity.

clarifyingQuestions.question: If multiple indices balance, which do I report?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The problem only asks existence (YES/NO), so the first match lets you return immediately.

examples.explanation: Single element: left sum = 0, right sum = 0. They're equal, so YES.
i=0: left 0 vs right 5. i=1: left 1 vs right 3. i=2: left 3 vs right 0. No index balances → NO.
At i=2 (value 3): left = 1+2 = 3, right = 3. Equal → YES.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recompute Both Sides
approaches.whenToMention: State it to fix the definition, then point out it re-sums the right side at every index for O(n²).
hints: For each candidate pivot i, what two quantities do you need to compare?
Sum the elements before i and the elements after i separately for every i.
Return YES the moment those two sums match; if no i works, return NO.
approaches.complexityReasoning: For each of n indices you sum up to n other elements → n·n/2 work, O(n²).
approaches.explanation:
The literal reading: for each index i, add up everything to its left, add up everything to its right, and compare.

**Why it's the natural baseline.** The problem is phrased per-index — 'is there an i where left equals right?' — so the obvious code loops over i and, inside, runs two more loops to build the two sums. It's plainly correct.

**The single-element case is free.** When n = 1, both inner loops run zero times, both sums are 0, and we return YES — no special casing needed.

**Why we don't ship it.** Re-summing the right side from scratch for every pivot repeats almost all the work. For n = 10⁵ that's ~5 billion additions per query and times out. The fix is to carry a running left sum and derive the right sum in O(1).
approaches.insight: Every iteration of the brute force recomputes a suffix sum that overlaps almost entirely with the previous iteration's. That redundancy is the signal to switch to a running prefix sum and a constant-time suffix derivation.

dryRun.intro: For each i, sum left and right explicitly and compare.

java.line: for (int l = 0; l < i; l++) left += arr[l];
java.explanation: Re-sum the entire left part — this inner loop is what makes it O(n²).
First balanced pivot answers the existence question immediately.

python.explanation: Slicing + sum rebuilds the prefix each step — quadratic overall.
Excludes arr[i]; the pivot is on neither side.

diagrams.caption: At i=2 the left part {1,2} and right part {3} are summed from scratch.

pitfalls: Including arr[i] in the left or right sum — the pivot belongs to neither.
Re-summing the suffix every iteration and timing out on 10⁵ inputs.
Returning NO for a single element — it's actually YES.

approaches.name: Running Prefix Sum (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want: one pass, O(1) space, suffix derived from the total.
hints: If you know the total of the whole array and the sum of everything to the left of i, can you get the right sum without another loop?
right = total − left − arr[i]. Keep left as a running accumulator as you sweep.
Compare left and right at each i; update left += arr[i] only after the comparison.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One pass to compute total, one pass to sweep — both O(n), with a couple of scalar variables → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Compute the total once. Then sweep left to right holding `left`, the sum of elements strictly before the current index. At index i the right side is everything except the left part and the pivot, so `right = total − left − arr[i]`. If `left == right`, return YES.

**Why the suffix is free.** The total never changes. Once you know how much sits to the left of i, the rest (minus the pivot) must be to the right. That's a subtraction, not a loop — so each index costs O(1) and the whole sweep is O(n).

**Why update left after the check.** The invariant is 'left = sum of indices 0..i−1'. At index i we compare *before* folding arr[i] in; only then do we add arr[i] so the invariant holds for i+1. Adding first would wrongly include the pivot in the left side.

**Single element and edges.** For n = 1, the loop checks i = 0 with left = 0 and right = total − 0 − arr[0] = 0 → YES. For the first index, left starts at 0 (empty prefix); for the last index, right computes to 0 (empty suffix). All handled by the same formula.

**Overflow note.** With n = 10⁵ and values up to 2×10⁴, the total can reach 2×10⁹ — just over the 32-bit signed limit. Use a 64-bit accumulator (long in Java) for total and left to be safe.
approaches.insight: The whole speedup is one identity: suffix = total − prefix − pivot. Recognizing that a suffix aggregate is recoverable from a global total and a running prefix is the reusable move — it powers equilibrium index, pivot-split, and 'can you partition into equal halves' questions alike.

Fold the pivot in AFTER comparing, so left stays 'sum strictly before next index'.

python.explanation: Derive the right side without a second loop.
Update after the check so the pivot is never on the left side during its own comparison.

edgeCases.behavior: i=0: right = 5 − 0 − 5 = 0, left = 0 → YES. Single element always balances.
i=0: left 0, right = 2 − 0 − 2 = 0 → YES. The pivot can be the first index with an empty left side.

pitfalls: Updating left before the comparison — pulls the pivot into the left side.
Using int for total/left — overflows near 2×10⁹.
Adding a second loop to compute the right sum — defeats the O(n) win.

commonMistakes: Counting the pivot element in one of the two sides.
Recomputing the right sum from scratch at every index (O(n²)).
Treating a single-element array as NO when it is YES.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Pivot included in a side
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The element at the chosen index belongs to neither side. Subtracting only left (not arr[i]) leaks the pivot into the right sum.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: long right = total - left;          // still includes arr[i]
commonMistakesDetailed.good: long right = total - left - arr[i]; // pivot excluded from both sides

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Updating the prefix too early
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you add arr[i] to left before comparing, left no longer represents 'strictly before i' and balanced pivots are missed.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for i, v in enumerate(arr):
    left += v
    right = total - left
    if left == right: return "YES"
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for v in arr:
    right = total - left - v
    if left == right: return "YES"
    left += v

commonMistakesDetailed.title: 32-bit overflow on the total
commonMistakesDetailed.why: n up to 10⁵ times values up to 2×10⁴ gives 2×10⁹, just past Integer.MAX_VALUE.

patternNote: Equilibrium / pivot via running prefix sum. Carry a prefix total and derive any suffix as total − prefix − current in O(1), collapsing a two-sided per-index comparison into a single linear sweep. Same trick behind Find Pivot Index and equilibrium-index problems.
